en: In order to enjoin [the disciple] to the meditation on Jñānaḍākinī, he says: "Listen.
He is called "Lord" (*prabhu*) because he possesses the power to enjoin his own disciples toward their welfare;
for this very reason, he "shines" (*rājate*).
He speaks of the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*).
"Avoidance," "relinquishing," and "separation" mean emptiness.
Of what? Of the state of duality. That is, of the state of duality such as existence and non-existence. That is what should be cultivated.
By whom? By one who knows the non-dual Dharma and is endowed with the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
How? By means of three [syllables], as stated in another tantra. Having uttered the three mantras beginning with "Śuddha," which are distinguished by the syllable *Oṃ* and the *svabhāvavajrayoga*s;

when? At the time when all yoga is the Knowledge-Ḍākinī (*jñānaḍākinī*), whose nature is the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*. Its first cause is the *vajra* together with *Hūṃ*; its "tip" (*agra*) is the commencement of bringing emptiness to face.

Note: Regarding the reading! One should recite "all yoga" (*sarvayoga*) and "the first and the foremost among them" (*ādimaṃ cāgraś ca teṣu*) in their respective order, namely *yogena* and so forth, *vajreṇa* and so forth, and *svabhāvena* and so forth.
The elision of the vowel *ā* in *agra* is etymological (*nairukta*).

The meaning is as follows: because they are devoid of the superimpositions of existence, non-existence, the grasped, the grasper, and so forth—by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), primordial essence (*prakṛti*), and emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—the aggregates (*skandha*) and other phenomena are pure and stainless; and I too am likewise, because I am included among all phenomena.
For it is said: "Vajra is emptiness; emptiness is called vajra. (cf. *Vajraśekhara*).
Because of that, they are pure due to the disappearance of all superimpositions of causal signs (*nimitta*).

Yoga is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); because it is devoid of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), it is pure. Since the grasping at a self is difficult to abandon, there are such statements as "I am pure by nature" (*svabhāvaśuddha*) and so forth.
However, by means of the three [concentrations], the three gateways to liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—are taught;
for even though [the mind] is pure by nature, these [three] serve to remove adventitious defilements.
Having acted thus—that is, having cultivated this—there is once again, specifically, that non-apprehension of all phenomena which has been previously abandoned.
Where is she situated? In places agreeable to the mind.
What is the nature of the meditation? He says: "Instantly," and so forth.
The connection is made by changing the case ending in the phrase "one should contemplate Jñānaḍākinī."
Thereafter, one should hold her in the sky,
preceded by worship.
By the word "the wise one" (matimān), he indicates other supreme methods such as the yoga of recollection mentioned elsewhere.
The ocean of gnosis is the wheel of deities beginning with the Jñāna-Ḍākinīs.
To the question "Having done what?", he says: "Mount Meru," and so forth.
Of that Mount Meru, there are four colors because it is composed of silver, sapphire, crystal, and gold, located in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions.

It was likewise in the primary directions; in the intermediate directions as well, they were of the same colors as the [primary] directions, because the intermediate directions are included within those respective directions. Contemplating what? The emergence from the golden peaked pavilion. The seven jewels: gold (*suvarṇa*), silver (*rūpya*), lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), musāragalva, agate (*aśmagarbha*), red pearl (*raktamukta*), and karketana. According to some, they are ruby (*padmarāga*), sapphire (*indranīla*), lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), emerald (*marataka*), diamond (*vajra*), pearl (*muktā*), and coral (*pravāla*).
"By expansions according to one's own wish" means an expansion dependent on one's own desire.
Immediately following this is the verse beginning with "vitāna," etc. (Sārdhagāthā 289v/582).
A banner marked with the lion and other such signs is a *dhvaja*.
In the eight directions, above, and below— thus in ten locations—
it is all-pervasive everywhere.
It is the fragrance-mandala, the collection of fragrances, within the interior of the peaked pavilion.
Regarding that, he describes the seat and so forth with the words beginning "lion" (*siṃha*).
That which breathes for oneself is the "breath" (*śvāsa*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), because it is the very nature of the vital energy (*prāṇa*); for this reason, it is meditated upon in the heart.
Having emerged and manifested through its transformation, he describes the nature of Jñānaḍākinī therein with the words beginning "three-faced" (*trimukha*).
Having placed the left foot upon one's own seat in the *paryaṅka* posture, one should extend the right leg slightly; this is the *sattvaparyaṅka*.
Here, all thirteen goddesses are seated in the *sattvaparyaṅka*.
Their crown-bands are bound and adorned with the radiating five Buddhas, and there is a vajra atop the crown.
She smiles with her right face, which is white; her root-face is wrathful with a loud, boisterous laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*); and her left face is red and amorous (*śṛṅgāra*). Each face has three eyes.
In her three right arms, she holds aloft a *khaṭvāṅga*, an axe, and a vajra; in her three left arms, a bell, a skull-cup, and a sword.
She is so described because she possesses a loud, terrifying laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*).
Regarding "of the vessels": a skull-cup filled with blood, which is the yoga-vessel, is held in the left hand. Vajraḍākinī and the others, possessing three eyes, gaze upon the central heroine.
"Of Jñāna" refers to Jñānaḍākinī.
"A lion in the mouth" means she has the face of a lion (Siṃhavaktrā).
"Lord of Nāgas" refers to an elephant.
In her right hand is a goad marked with a vajra;
in her left is a noose with the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
The three [other goddesses], beginning with Vyāghrī, have the faces of a tiger, a jackal, and an owl.
"Nāga" refers to the eight lords of serpents; the singular number is used here to denote the class. "Of that very serpent" means of that very snake. "Rājendrī" is her name.
The consort is named Rājendrī;
"of the hands" means two hands in the form of an *añjali*.
Regarding "of the two hands in *añjali*": she displays the *añjali* of the two hands above her head in the shape of a lamp.
"By means of a red thread," and so forth: with the two hands joined in the *añjali* gesture and raised upward, she drinks blood as if by a stream, like a red thread.

"The index fingers [forming] a trident in the hands": having formed the *vajra-añjali* with both hands and joined the tips of the two thumbs together, the two index fingers are made into a needle, which is thus called a "trident.
That, moreover, is held at her own private parts (*bhaga*).
"Causing delusion" means bewildering all minds and bringing them under one's control; this is the meaning. He concludes: "The All-Knowing One should meditate on everything.
In this way, the yogi who knows all the colors, symbols, and so forth, should meditate upon the entire mandala.
Like the lion throne, the other seats as well are occupied by the sun.
In every instance, the goddesses are the transformations of their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
With these [mantras], and so forth: one should display the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*) for each of these goddesses according to its own specific form.
He extracts the seed-syllable of Jñānaḍākinī: "anilānalasaptatva" means that it is distinguished by being above the "wind," which is the wind-mandala or half-moon;
from the letter *ra* of "fire" (*anala*), the seventh is the letter *ha*, joined below with the letter *ū*, the seed-syllable of Vajrī.
Above the half-moon, it is conjoined with the bindu and nāda; thus, "hūṃ" arises.
And that syllable *hūṃ* rains down a stream of bodhicitta, hence it is called "downpouring the stream.
By this, he indicates the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*).
This is the meaning:

in a certain place favorable to the mind, facing westward with hair loosened, preceded by the offering of a *bali* oblation, one should instantly resolve that oneself has the form of Jñānaḍākinī. Having summoned Jñānaḍākinī together with her retinue into the sky by means of rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and having worshipped her with both external and internal offerings through goddesses born from the seed-syllable in the heart, one should meditate on everything from the confession of sins up to equanimity. Then, reciting the internal mantra—“Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature”—one should contemplate its meaning.
Having brought this to mind, one should enter into the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*).
Then, with the mantra *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*, one should visualize the ground as consisting of vajras. With *oṃ jambhani hūṃ phaṭ*, one visualizes the vajra-fence, and with *oṃ juṃ svāhā*, the vajra-canopy.

Having expelled the obstructors with "Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ," in the center thereof, upon Vāyu, Agni, Ambu, Pṛthvī, and Sumeru—arisen respectively from the syllables Vuṃ, Kṣuṃ, Suṃ, Huṃ, and Hūṃ—is a golden gabled temple (kūṭāgāra) inlaid with the seven precious gems, transformed from "Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ. In its center and in the four directions, upon five lions and world-lotuses, are five discs of the sun; and upon the central lion is a white parasol.

Therein, having meditated upon a vajra situated in the center of the moon and sun born from the *ālikāli* [vowels and consonants], presided over by the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, one should recite: "Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure; I am vajra-pure. Then, after those Tathāgatas and goddesses emanated therefrom have accomplished the welfare of the world, and upon their reabsorption, one should visualize Jñānaḍākinī as perfected by the moon and other elements, and simultaneously with her arising, visualize the members of the maṇḍala also arisen from their respective seed-syllables. One should then cultivate the divine pride, thinking: "Oṃ, all phenomena are yoga-pure; I am yoga-pure."

Therein, upon the suns of the universal lotuses that serve as the respective seats of Vajraḍākinī and the others, there are, in due order, the seed-syllables *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, *āṃ īṃ ūṃ ṝṃ ḹṃ aiṃ auṃ aḥ*.
All thirteen goddesses should be visualized with disheveled hair, adorned with snakes, and possessing the colors, weapons, and other attributes as previously described.

There, having placed *kṣuṃ* upon the crown of one’s own head; *huṃ* in the eyes; *yuṃ* in the ears and nostrils; *suṃ* on the tongues; *smryuṃ* on the neck; *hmryuṃ* at the roots of the arms; *ymryuṃ* in the heart; and *kṣmryuṃ* at the navel; and having placed the armor-syllables (*kavaca*) of Ghorī, Caṇḍālī, Vettālī, Vajraḍākinī, Siṃhinī, Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Ulūkī in their respective order; and having performed the consecration of body, speech, and mind with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*;
one should summon the Wisdom Circle (*jñānacakra*) by means of light rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, worship it duly in the sky, and display the pledge (*samaya*).
There, having formed two vajra-fists and extending the two middle fingers so that their tips touch, one should show [this mudrā] while reciting "Oṃ hūṃ svāhā" for Jñānaḍākinī.
Having formed the vajra-añjali, repeatedly touching and moving the two middle fingers with the two elder thumbs, one offers it to Vajraḍākinī while reciting "Oṃ vajraḍākinī hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having formed two fists equally and extending the two elder thumbs, one offers it to Ghorī while reciting "Oṃ ghorī hūṃ svāhā."

Having formed this very mudrā, one should extend both little fingers; [reciting] *oṃ vettālī hūṃ svāhā* for Vettālī. Having formed this very mudrā, while extending both middle fingers, [reciting] *oṃ caṇḍālī hūṃ svāhā* for Caṇḍālī.
Having formed two vajra-fists and extended both index fingers, touching their tips together, [recite] *oṃ āṃ svāhā*, *oṃ īṃ svāhā*, *oṃ ūṃ svāhā*, and *oṃ ṝṃ svāhā* for the four beginning with Siṃhī.
Extending both hands in the form of *añjali* and placing them at the mouth, one says "oṃ ḷṃ svāhā" for Rājendrī.
Holding the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed cupped hands) upon the head, one says "oṃ aiṃ svāhā" for Dīpinī.
Raising the *añjali* and placing it near the face, one says "oṃ auṃ svāhā" for Cūṣiṇī.

Having performed the lotus-turning (*kamalāvartana*) with both hands and maintaining the vajra-añjali, one should place [the deity] as before in the position of the vulva while reciting *oṃ aḥ svāhā* for Kāmbojī.
Thereafter, preceded by the lotus-turning, one should cause the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*) to enter the commitment-wheel (*samayacakra*) according to the proper application.
Then, one should contemplate the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the sealing (*mudraṇa*).

In that regard, Jñānaḍākinī and the others are [sealed] respectively by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi; Siṃhī and the others by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, and Amitābha; and Rājendrī and the others by Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.

Thereafter, having worshipped oneself with the goddesses of emanated offerings and having offered praise, one should taste the nectar presented by them. Then, one should visualize the syllable *HŪṂ*—situated upon a moon-maṇḍala within the lotus of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), facing downward, and joined to a drop (*bindu*) between the eyebrows—as a downpour of streams through the flowing stream of nectar. Following this subtle yoga of the internalized drop (*antarbhāvitabinduyoga*), when weariness arises, one should recite the mantra *Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā* three hundred thousand times; furthermore, by reciting the mantras of Vajraḍākinī and the others that will be described hereafter, one attains the desired accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The tenth mañjarī in the Sampuṭa-ṭīkā, the Āmnāyamañjarī.
